cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XXIII
The bed;\nthe test that Penelope wins; the long night held back.
And the old woman climbed to\nthe upper room, laughing aloud,
to tell her mistress that her own\ndear husband was in the house;
her knees were pumping fast, her feet stumbled with hurry.
She stood over Penelope's head and spoke to her:
"Wake, Penelope, dear child — so you can see with\nyour own eyes what you have longed for all your days!
Odysseus is here — he has come home — however late.
And he has killed the lordly suitors, the men who plagued
his house, and ate his goods, and bullied his son."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her:
"Dear nurse, the gods have made you mad. The gods\ncan strike even the full of sense to foolishness,
and set the empty-headed on the road of wisdom:
they have unstrung you. Your mind was straight before.
Why do you mock me, when my heart is all one grief,\ntelling wild tales — and shake me out of the sleep,
the sweet sleep that had bound me,\nfolding my eyelids under?
I have not slept so sound since the day Odysseus\nwent to look on Evil-Ilium, never to be named.
Go on — down with you now, back to the hall.
If any other of my women had come to me with\nnews like this, and shaken me out of sleep,
I would soon have sent her packing back to the hall
and roughly. You — your old\nage spares you that, at least."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered her:
"I do not mock you, dear child. It is true:
Odysseus is here — he has come home, just as I tell you —
the stranger, the one they all dishonored in the hall.
Telemachus knew long since that he was here,\nbut kept his father's purposes hidden, cool of head,
till he should punish the violence\nof those overbearing men."
So she spoke; and Penelope, all joy, sprang out of bed
and clung to the old woman,\ntears spilling from her eyelids,
and lifting her voice she spoke winged words to her:
"Come then, dear nurse — tell me truly:
if he has really come home, as you say he has,\nhow did he lay his hands on the shameless suitors —
one man alone, when they were always in there in a pack?"
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered her:
"I did not see, I did not ask. I heard only the groaning
of men being killed. We sat in\nthe corner of our strong-built
quarters, struck dumb —\nthe close-fitted doors held us in —
until the hour your son called me out of the hall,\nTelemachus: his father had sent him to call me.
And then I found Odysseus standing among the bodies of\nthe slain; and they, around him, on the trodden floor
lay heaped on one another.\nIt would have warmed your heart —
Now they are all together at the courtyard gates,\nand he is purging the beautiful house with sulfur,
and has built a great fire; and he sent me to call you.
Come with me now — so both of you can set your dear hearts
in the way of gladness at last:\nyou have suffered so much evil.
Now, this time, the long desire is accomplished:
he has come himself, alive,\nto his own hearth; and he has found you
and his son still in the halls;\nand the men who wronged him,
the suitors — he has punished them all in his own house."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her:
"Dear nurse — no crowing yet. Hold back your laughter.
You know how welcome the sight of him would be to\neveryone in this house — most of all to me and to our son.
But this tale cannot be true, not as you tell it:
no — some one of the immortals\nhas killed the lordly suitors,
outraged at their heart-stinging\ninsolence and their evil deeds.
For they honored nobody on this earth,\nbad man or good, whoever came among them;
so through their own blind folly\nthey have suffered. But Odysseus —
far away he has lost his homecoming,\nlost out of Achaea; he himself is lost."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered her:
"My child, what a word has\nslipped the fence of your teeth!
Your husband is here —\nat his own hearthside — and you declare
he will never come home!\nYour heart was always unbelieving.
Come then — I will give you another sign, and a plain one:
the scar the boar dealt him long ago with its white tusk.
I found it as I washed him, and I wanted to tell you —
you yourself — but he clapped his hand across my mouth
and would not let me speak: his mind is full of cunning.
But come. And I will stake my own life on it:
if I am deceiving you, kill me by\nthe most pitiful death there is."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her:
"Dear nurse — the counsels of the gods who are forever:
it is hard for you to fathom them,\nsharp-witted as you are.
But even so, let us go down to my son, so I may see\nthe suitors dead — and the man who killed them."
So speaking she went down from\nthe upper room; and her heart
churned: should she question her\ndear husband from a distance,
or go to him, and take his head and hands, and kiss them?
And when she came in, and crossed the stone threshold,
she sat down opposite Odysseus, in the light of the fire,
against the other wall. And he, by the tall pillar,\nsat looking at the ground, waiting to learn whether
his strong-built wife would speak\nto him, once her eyes had seen.
But she sat a long while silent,\nwonder flooding her heart:
with her eyes now she would gaze at him, full in the face;
now fail to know him — in the bad clothes on his body.
And Telemachus rebuked her,\nand spoke a word, and named her:
"Mother mine — no mother! — with your unbending heart,\nwhy do you hold apart from my father so? Why not
sit close beside him, and question him,\nand ask him everything?
No other woman would harden her heart like this,\nand stand apart from a husband who, after suffering much,
came in the twentieth year to his own fatherland.
But your heart is harder than stone —\nas it has always been."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"My child, the heart in my breast is stunned to stillness:
I cannot speak one word to him, cannot ask a question,\ncannot look him in the face. But if he is truly
Odysseus — if he has come home — then surely we two
shall know one another,\nand better than anyone: for we have
signs between us — hidden signs,\nthat we two know and no one else."
So she spoke; and much-enduring noble Odysseus smiled,\nand quickly he spoke winged words to Telemachus:
"Telemachus — let your mother test me in the\nhalls as she will: she will soon see more clearly.
Now, because I am filthy,\nand the clothes on my body are bad,
she holds me cheap, and will not yet say I am the man.
But we — let us think how this can come out best.
For a man who has killed even one man in the land —\none man, with few behind him to avenge him after —
goes into exile, leaving his kin and his fathers' country.
And we have killed the prop of the city —\nfar the noblest of the young men in Ithaca.
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"You look to it yourself, dear father. Yours,\nthey say, is the best mind among mankind: no mortal man
could set himself against you there.
As for us — we are with you,\nblazing for it; and I say we shall not
come short in courage, such strength as is in us."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Then I will say how it seems best to me.
First: bathe yourselves, and put clean tunics on,\nand tell the serving-women in the halls to dress;
and let the godlike singer,\nwith the clear lyre in his hands,
lead us all in the steps of the playful dance —
so that anyone who hears it from\noutside will say, 'A wedding!' —
a passer-by on the road,\nor one of our neighbors round about —
so that the wide rumor of the suitors' killing does\nnot run down through the town before we can get away
out to our orchard-farm among the trees. There, after,
we shall see what profit the\nOlympian puts into our hands."
So he spoke; and they listened well and obeyed.
First they bathed themselves, and put clean tunics on,\nand the women dressed; and the godlike singer took up
the hollow lyre, and woke in all of them the craving\nfor the sweetness of song and the blameless dance.
And the great house rang around them to the footfalls\nof men at play and fair-belted women dancing;
and a man would say, hearing it from outside the house:
"So! Someone has married the much-wooed queen at last.
Hard woman — she had not the heart to keep her wedded
husband's great house through to the end, until he came."
So a man would say. And they\ndid not know how things stood.
And meanwhile, inside his house, great-hearted Odysseus
was bathed by the housekeeper\nEurynome, and rubbed with oil,
and she put a beautiful mantle round him, and a tunic;
and over him, from the head down,\nAthena poured great beauty:
taller to look at, and broader, and down from his head
she made the locks flow in curls,\nlike the hyacinth flower.
As when a man lays gold over silver — a craftsman\nwhom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught
art of every kind, and he finishes works full of grace —\nso she poured grace over his head and shoulders.
Out of the bath he came, in build like the immortals,
and sat back down on the chair from which he had risen,\nopposite his wife, and spoke his word to her:
"Strange woman! To you beyond all womankind the\ndwellers on Olympus gave an unyielding heart.
No other woman would harden her heart like this,\nand stand apart from a husband who, after suffering much,
came in the twentieth year to his own fatherland.
Well then, nurse — make me up a bed, so I can lie down
by myself at least. The heart\nin this one's breast is iron."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Strange man! I am not being proud,\nand I am not slighting you —
nor am I too much amazed. I know very well what you\nwere when you went from Ithaca on your long-oared ship.
Well then — Eurycleia: make up the packed bedstead for him
outside the well-built bridal chamber — the bed he made
with his own hands. Move the\npacked bedstead out there for him,
and pile the bedding on: the fleeces,\nthe cloaks, the shining blankets."
So she spoke — testing her husband. And Odysseus\nflared out in anger at his true-hearted wife:
"Woman — that is a wounding word you have spoken!
Who has set my bed somewhere else? That would be hard
even for a skilled workman — unless a god in person came
and set it down, at his easy will, in some other place:
no living mortal man, not one in his best young strength,
could lightly lever it aside. For a great sign is built
into that worked bed — and I made it: I, no other man.
A bush of olive grew inside the\ncourtyard fence, long-leaved,
full-grown and flourishing, its trunk thick as a pillar.
Around it I built our chamber,\nand I worked at it till it was done —
close-set stone; and I roofed it well above,\nand hung the jointed doors on it, close-fitting.
Then — and only then — I cut back\nthe long-leaved olive's crown,
trimmed the trunk up from the root,\nand with the bronze I planed it
smooth all round, with skill, and trued it to the line:
a bedpost worked from the living tree.\nAnd I bored it all with the auger,
and starting from that post I planed\nout the bed, until I finished,
inlaying it with gold and silver and ivory,
and I stretched across its frame an\noxhide strap, bright with crimson.
There is our sign — I show it to you. What I do not know,
woman, is whether my bed still stands fast, or by now
some man has cut the olive off at the root and moved it."
So he spoke; and her knees went slack\nwhere she sat, and her dear heart,
as she recognized the tokens Odysseus described so surely;
and bursting into tears she ran straight to him, and threw
her arms around Odysseus' neck,\nand kissed his head, and said:
"Do not be angry with me, Odysseus — you who in everything
understood the most of men.\nIt was the gods who gave us sorrow —
the gods, who begrudged that we two, staying side by side,
should have the joy of our youth\nand come to the doorsill of old age.
But do not be angry with me now, do not hold it against me
that at first, when I saw you,\nI did not welcome you like this.
For always the heart here in my breast kept shivering:
terror that some man would come\nand cheat me with his talk —
and men enough there are who plot such wicked profits.
Not even Argive Helen, daughter of Zeus, would have\njoined in love and bed with a man from another land
had she known that the warlike sons of the Achaeans\nwould carry her home again to her own dear country.
A god it was who stirred her\nto the shameful thing she did;
and not until too late that she laid to heart that folly,
the ruinous folly from which\ngrief first came — to us as well.
But now — now you have told over the plain tokens of\nour own bed, which no other mortal has laid eyes on:
only you and I, and one single serving-woman, Actoris,\nwhom my father gave me when I first came here,
who kept the door of our close-built bridal chamber —\nnow you persuade my heart, unbending as it is."
So she spoke; and in him she stirred\na still greater longing to weep,
and he wept, holding the wife of\nhis heart, the true, the steadfast.
And as when land shows welcome to men swimming for it —\nmen whose well-made ship Poseidon has smashed
on the open sea, driving it under wind and heavy wave,
and few of them swim clear of the gray sea to the shore,\ntheir bodies caked with all the brine of it,
and glad at last they step on land, escaped from evil:
so welcome was her husband to her,\nas her eyes gazed at him,
and she could not once let her\nwhite arms go from his neck.
And Dawn of the fingers of rose\nwould have risen on their weeping,
had not the goddess thought of\none thing more — gray-eyed Athena:
she held the long night back\nat the world's edge, and penned
gold-throned Dawn at Ocean, and would not let her yoke\nher quick-footed horses that carry the light to men,
Lampus and Phaethon, the colts that draw the Dawn.
And then Odysseus of the many designs spoke to his wife:
"Lady — we have not yet come to the end of every trial:
there is still to be one labor past all measure,\nlong and hard, and I must carry it through to the last.
For so the ghost of Teiresias prophesied to\nme the day I went down into the house of Hades
seeking a homecoming for my companions and myself.
But come, wife — let us go to bed, so that at last\nwe can lie down and take the sweetness of our sleep."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Your bed is there for you whenever your heart\nwishes it — now that the gods have brought you home
to your own well-built house and your fathers' land.
But since you have thought of it —\nsince a god has put it in your heart —
come, tell me the trial: for I shall hear of it later\nanyway, I think, and it is no worse to know it now."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Strange woman — why do you press me so, and order\nme to speak? Well, I will tell it, and hide nothing.
Your heart will take no joy in it; no more does mine:
for he ordered me on through many towns of mortals yet,\ntraveling with a well-shaped oar in my hands,
until I come to men who know nothing of the sea,\nmen who eat no food that is mixed with salt,
who know nothing of red-cheeked ships, nothing\nof well-shaped oars, which are wings for ships.
And he told me a sign, unmistakable.\nI will not hide it from you:
when another traveler, meeting me on the road,\nsays I carry a winnowing-fan on my shining shoulder,
then and there he ordered me to fix the oar in the\nearth and offer fine victims to the lord Poseidon —
a ram, a bull, and a boar that has mounted sows —\nand turn away home, and offer holy hecatombs
to the deathless gods who hold wide heaven,\nto all of them, each in order. And death will come to me
from the sea, so gentle a death, and take me worn\ndown under sleek old age; and around me the peoples
will be prosperous. All this,\nhe said, will be accomplished."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"If the gods are really bringing on a better old age,
then there is hope there will\nbe an escape from our evils."
So they spoke to one another of such things.
And meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse made up the bed
with soft coverings, under the light of blazing torches.
And when they had spread the\npacked bedstead, working quickly,
the old woman went away to her own room to sleep,\nand Eurynome the chamber-woman led them on
their way to bed, a torch in her hands;\nshe brought them to the chamber, and went back. And they —
glad, they came to the rite of their own old bed.
And Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd\nrested their feet from the dance, and rested the women,
and lay down to sleep themselves\nthrough the shadowy halls.
And when the two had taken their\nfill of the loveliness of love,
they took their pleasure in words,\ntelling each other everything:
she, the shining among women, all she had endured in\nthe halls, watching that deadly crowd of suitor-men
who on her account kept slaughtering so many beasts,
oxen and fat sheep, while the wine\ndrained out of the jars by the vatful;
and Zeus-born Odysseus, all the sorrows he had dealt
to other men, and all he had\ntoiled through in his own grief —
he told it all; and she delighted in the listening,
and no sleep fell upon her eyelids\ntill he had told everything.
He began with how he beat the Cicones first, and came\nfrom there to the rich plowland of the Lotus-eaters;
and all the Cyclops did,\nand how he took the price from him
for the brave companions he had eaten without pity;\nand how he came to Aeolus, who received him kindly
and sent him on — but it was not yet his portion to reach
his own dear country: the storm-wind snatched him up again
and drove him, groaning heavily, over the fish-filled sea;
and how he came to Telepylus of the Laestrygonians,
who destroyed his ships and all\nhis strong-greaved companions —
all of them: Odysseus alone got clear in his black ship;\nand he told her Circe's guile and her many wiles,
and how he went down into the dank house of\nHades to consult the ghost of Theban Teiresias,
in his many-benched ship, and saw all his companions,
and his mother, who bore him and\nreared him when he was little;
and how he heard the voice of the thronging Sirens,\nand came to the Clashing Rocks, and dread Charybdis,
and Scylla, whom men have never yet slipped past unhurt;
and how his companions killed the cattle of the Sun;\nand how Zeus who thunders on high struck the fast ship
with a smoking bolt, and his brave companions perished\nall together — and he alone escaped the evil fates;
and how he came to the island\nof Ogygia and the nymph Calypso,
who kept him there, aching to have him for her husband,\nin her hollow caves, and fed him, and kept promising
to make him deathless and ageless all his days —\nyet she never persuaded the heart in his breast;
and how, after much suffering, he came to the Phaeacians,\nwho honored him from the heart, like a god,
and sent him home with a ship to his own dear country,\nwith gifts of bronze and gold and clothing in plenty.
That was the last word he spoke, as the sweet sleep
that unstrings the limbs leapt on him,\nloosing the cares of his heart.
Then the goddess thought of one\nthing more, gray-eyed Athena:
when she judged that Odysseus in his heart had taken\nhis fill of the bed of his wife, and his fill of sleep,
at once she roused the gold-throned\nearly-born one out of Ocean,
to carry her light to mankind. And Odysseus rose\nfrom the soft bed, and laid this charge on his wife:
"Lady — by now we have had our fill of trials,\nthe two of us both: you here, weeping over
my homecoming with all its cares,\nwhile Zeus and the other gods
nailed me in pain far from my own country, straining home.
Now that we both have come to the bed we longed for,\nyou must care for the property I have inside the halls;
as for the flocks the overweening suitors wasted —\nmany I will raid back myself, and the Achaeans
will give the rest, until they fill up every fold.
But now I am going out to the orchard-farm and its trees,
to see my noble father, who grieves for me so hard.
And on you, wife, I lay this charge — wise as you are:
with the rising sun the story will be out and running —\nthe suitors, the men I killed here in the halls.
Go up to the upper room with your attendant women\nand sit there. Look at no one. Ask no questions."
He spoke, and drew the beautiful armor over his shoulders,
and roused Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd,
and told them all to take up\nweapons of war in their hands.
They did not disobey: they harnessed themselves in bronze,
and opened the doors, and went out; and Odysseus led.
By now the light was over the earth; but Athena hid\nthem in night, and led them quickly out of the town.
